title: Cassiopeia
tagline: The northern queen whose five bright stars form the sky's most recognizable W.
intro: On a clear night in the northern hemisphere, look toward the pole and you'll find her — a jagged W (or, when she tumbles, an M) of five stars that never quite leave the sky. Cassiopeia is both a myth and a map: a vain queen bound to her throne, and a bright signpost to nebulae, clusters and the Milky Way's Perseus Arm.

whyFutura.title: Why Futura wears her W
whyFutura.prose: Futura is built for looking ahead — toward IPOs, growth, SpaceX and Tesla, and whatever comes next. Our quiet motto is looking higher. Cassiopeia felt like the right companion for that: a northern guide star of a constellation, always somewhere above the horizon for most of us who built this, and a shape you can draw with five points and a few thin lines. The W is restrained, precise and a little mythic. We use it as the wordmark and as a quiet motif behind the pages — a reminder that the long view is older than any ticker.

mythology.title: The queen on her throne
mythology.prose: In Greek myth, Cassiopeia was queen of Aethiopia, wife of King Cepheus and mother of Andromeda. She boasted that she — and in some tellings her daughter — was more beautiful than the Nereids, the sea nymphs. Poseidon answered the insult by sending the sea monster Cetus to ravage the coast, and demanded Andromeda as sacrifice. Perseus arrived in time, rescued her, and later the whole family was set among the stars: Cepheus the king, Andromeda the princess, Perseus the hero, Cetus the beast — and Cassiopeia herself, bound to a throne that circles the north celestial pole. For half of each day she hangs upside down, a celestial reminder of vanity. That is why the same five stars read as a dignified W when high in autumn evenings, and as a tipping M when she swings under the pole.

observing.title: Where and when to find her
observing.prose: Cassiopeia sits opposite the Big Dipper across Polaris, roughly at right ascension 1h and declination +60°. From mid-northern latitudes she is circumpolar — she never sets. Step outside in autumn and early winter evenings and she is high and obvious; in spring she skims lower toward the northern horizon. From the southern hemisphere she is a winter visitor low in the north, or not visible at all from far south. The W is naked-eye easy under suburban skies; under dark skies the Milky Way pours through her, and binoculars fill the field with clusters.

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: W when upright; M when she tips under the pole

stars.title: The five stars of the W
stars.intro: West to east when the W is upright (Caph → Schedar → Navi → Ruchbah → Segin), the asterism spans stars that look alike to the eye and are anything but alike in life. Brightness order on a typical night is Schedar, Caph, Gamma Cas, Ruchbah, then the fainter Segin — except when Gamma Cas flares and briefly claims the throne.

items.name: Caph
items.fact: The nearest of the five, and a Delta Scuti pulsator — a white giant that quietly expands and contracts, changing brightness by a few hundredths of a magnitude.

items.name: Schedar
items.fact: An orange giant — the W's warm ember. Her name comes from the Arabic şadr, "chest," for the queen's heart; at ~45 solar radii she is the largest of the five.

items.name: Navi
items.fact: A Be star and the prototype of the Gamma Cassiopeiae variables: a fast spinner (~432 km/s) that flings off a glowing disk and can outshine Schedar when she flares. "Navi" is Ivan backwards — a nickname for astronaut Virgil Ivan "Gus" Grissom.

items.name: Ruchbah
items.fact: A white subgiant, and likely an Algol-type eclipsing binary — dips in brightness have been timed to a ~759-day orbit between the two components.

items.name: Segin
items.fact: The faintest point of the W and still a young, hot blue main-sequence star (~15 million years old, ~9 solar masses) that will burn through the rest of her life in only a few more million years.

deepSky.title: Deep-sky companions
deepSky.intro: Cassiopeia's corner of the Milky Way is crowded with nurseries and clusters. A few favorites near the W:

items.name: Heart Nebula
items.blurb: A sprawling emission nebula east of Segin, shaped like a cosmic heart and lit by the massive stars of Melotte 15 at its center. Often photographed with its neighbor, the Soul.

sources.label: BBC Sky at Night: Heart and Soul

items.name: Soul Nebula
items.blurb: Also called the Baby Nebula — a star-forming cloud about 2½° southeast of the Heart, carved by winds from young clusters within.

sources.label: BBC Sky at Night: Heart and Soul

items.name: Owl / E.T. Cluster
items.blurb: Two bright "eyes" and chains of fainter stars that look like an owl — or, to a generation of observers, like E.T. Find it about 2° south of Ruchbah; easy in binoculars.

items.name: Pacman Nebula
items.blurb: An emission nebula just east of Schedar whose dark dust lane forms Pac-Man's mouth. A classic wide-field imaging target, discovered by E.E. Barnard in 1883.
